title: Containers versus VMs
summary: Why containers are light, what isolates them, and the states a container moves through.

steps.title: Not a tiny virtual machine
body: A **virtual machine** emulates hardware and boots a whole guest operating system with its own kernel. A **container** is just a set of ordinary processes on the host, fenced off by Linux kernel features:
- **namespaces** give the processes their own view of process IDs, network, hostname and filesystem mounts;
- **cgroups** cap how much CPU and memory they may use.
```text
virtual machines                       containers
│ app A  ││ app B  ││ app C  │     │ app A  ││ app B  ││ app C  │
│ libs   ││ libs   ││ libs   │     │ libs   ││ libs   ││ libs   │
│ hypervisor                   │   │ host OS + ONE shared kernel  │
│ hardware                     │   │ hardware                     │

No kernel to boot means a container starts in milliseconds and an image can be a few megabytes. The trade-off: all containers share the host kernel, so isolation is weaker than a VM. On Windows and macOS, Docker Desktop quietly runs one small Linux VM and puts your containers inside it.

steps.prompt: Why does `docker run alpine echo hi` finish in well under a second, when booting a VM takes much longer?
options: The container is just a process on the already-running host kernel; nothing has to boot
Alpine is cached in RAM by the hypervisor
Docker skips the BIOS but still boots a small kernel
Echo commands are executed by Docker itself, not inside the container
steps.explain: A container is a fenced-off process. Starting it costs about as much as starting the process, plus setting up namespaces.

steps.prompt: Which describes a **virtual machine** and which a **container**?
items: Can run a Windows guest on a Linux host
Image is often tens of megabytes
steps.explain: A Linux container uses the host's Linux kernel, so it cannot run a different OS kernel. A VM can, because it brings its own.

steps.title: The container lifecycle
body: A container moves through a few states:
```text
docker create          docker start
docker stop / kill,       │    │ docker start
or the main process exits ▼    │ docker restart
exited
docker rm     ▼
(removed)
- `docker run` is a shortcut for **create + start** (plus a pull if the image is missing).
- A container lives exactly as long as its **main process** (PID 1). When that process ends, for any reason, the container is `exited`.
- An exited container still exists: its writable layer and logs are kept until you `docker rm` it.
- `docker rm` refuses a running container unless you add `-f`.

steps.prompt: Put the commands in an order that takes a container from nothing to gone, using each state once.
steps.explain: create → created, start → running, stop → exited, rm → removed. `docker rm` would fail on a running container.

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it does to a container.
pairs: makes a container from an image, but does not start it
runs the main process of an existing container
sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period
deletes a stopped container and its writable layer

steps.prompt: You run `docker run --name once alpine echo hi`. A minute later, what state is the `once` container in?
options: exited, because its main process (`echo`) finished
running, because containers keep running until stopped
created, because it was never started
steps.explain: PID 1 was `echo`. It printed and ended, so the container exited. It is still listed by `docker ps -a` until you remove it (or you pass `--rm`).

steps.prompt: Continuing: you run the command below. What does it print?
steps.explain: Docker keeps what the main process wrote to stdout and stderr, even after the container exited. `docker logs` replays it.

steps.title: Walk a container through its lifecycle
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. `docker ps -a` shows two containers: `web` was **created** but never
1. Start `web` (do not create a new one).
2. Run a one-off container named `job` from `busybox:1.37` that prints `migrated` and exits. Keep it afterwards
(no `--rm`), so its exit code and log can be read.

checks.name: web is running (the same container that was created)
checks.fail: `web` is not running, or it is a new container. `docker start web` starts the one that exists.

checks.name: job exited with code 0 and printed migrated
checks.cmd: test "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' job)" = 'exited 0' && docker logs job | grep -qx migrated
checks.fail: There should be an exited container `job` (exit code 0) whose log is `migrated`. `docker run --name job busybox:1.37 echo migrated`.

checks.name: old is removed
checks.fail: `old` still exists. An exited container stays until `docker rm` removes it.

hints: `docker start NAME` starts a created or stopped container; `docker run` would make a new one.
`docker run` without `-d` waits for the command, so a one-off job ends as `Exited (0)` in `docker ps -a`.
`docker rm old` removes an exited container (`-f` would also stop a running one first).
solution: docker run --name job busybox:1.37 echo migrated
steps.explain: Created, running, exited and removed are real states of one object: `start` moved the same container on, `run` created and started a new one, and an exited container kept its log and exit code until `rm`. That is why `docker ps -a` fills up on a dev box, and why one-off jobs usually get `--rm`.
